items.followUp: Why does a true solution form a homogeneous mixture?

rubric.why: Identifies why the suspension particles do not make a uniform solution.
rubric.description: States that suspension particles are relatively large or do not dissolve in the solvent.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the particles are large or insoluble.

rubric.why: Explains that the suspension is not uniform throughout.
rubric.description: States that the particles may settle or that the suspension is heterogeneous or non-uniform.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying settling or lack of uniformity.

modelAnswer: A suspension does not form a homogeneous mixture because its relatively large particles do not dissolve in the solvent.
The particles remain separate and may settle on standing, so the composition is not uniform throughout; the suspension is heterogeneous.

items.followUp: State three observations from Rutherford’s alpha-particle scattering experiment and give two limitations of his atomic model.

rubric.why: Identifies the main observation that most alpha particles passed through the foil.
rubric.description: States that most alpha particles passed through the gold foil without deflection.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for this observation.

rubric.why: Identifies the observation that a small number of alpha particles changed direction slightly.
rubric.description: States that a few alpha particles were deflected through small angles.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for this observation.

rubric.why: Identifies the rare backward scattering of alpha particles.
rubric.description: States that very few alpha particles were deflected backwards, bounced back or were reflected.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for this observation.

rubric.why: Tests whether the student identifies the model’s failure to account for atomic stability.
rubric.description: States that Rutherford’s model could not explain atomic stability, or that orbiting electrons should radiate energy and fall into the nucleus.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for this defect.

rubric.why: Tests whether the student identifies the model’s failure to explain atomic spectra.
rubric.description: States that Rutherford’s model could not explain the line spectra of atoms.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for this defect.

modelAnswer: Three results of Rutherford’s alpha-particle scattering experiment were:
Most alpha particles passed through the gold foil without any deflection.
A few alpha particles were deflected through small angles.
Very few alpha particles were deflected backwards or bounced back.
Two defects of Rutherford’s atomic model were:
It could not explain atomic stability: revolving electrons should radiate energy and fall into the nucleus.
It could not explain the line spectra of atoms.

items.followUp: Define a molecular ion and give three differences between a molecule and a molecular ion.

rubric.why: Checks the defining idea that a molecular ion is a group of atoms with a net charge.
rubric.description: Defines a molecular ion as a bonded group of atoms that carries a charge.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating both that it is a group of atoms and that it is charged.

rubric.why: Checks the fundamental difference in net electrical charge.
rubric.description: Contrasts the neutral charge of a molecule with the net charge of a molecular ion.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for this comparison.

rubric.why: Checks the difference in how the two are represented, with a neutral formula versus an ion formula carrying a charge sign.
rubric.description: Shows that a molecular formula has no charge sign, whereas a molecular-ion formula includes one; suitable examples also earn credit.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct comparison or examples such as H₂O and NH₄⁺.

rubric.why: Checks the electron-transfer explanation for the charge on a molecular ion.
rubric.description: States that gaining electrons gives a negative molecular ion or losing electrons gives a positive molecular ion.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for either correct electron-transfer relationship.

modelAnswer: A molecular ion is a bonded group of two or more atoms that carries a net electric charge.
Three differences between a molecule and a molecular ion are:
A molecule is electrically neutral, whereas a molecular ion has a positive or negative net charge.
A molecular formula has no charge sign, whereas a molecular-ion formula includes its charge sign; for example, H₂O is neutral and NH₄⁺ is a molecular ion.
A molecular ion becomes charged when the bonded group gains electrons (negative charge) or loses electrons (positive charge).

items.followUp: Explain the formation of the coordinate covalent bond in the hydronium ion, H₃O⁺.

rubric.why: Checks the defining feature that one atom supplies both electrons in the shared pair.
rubric.description: Defines a coordinate covalent bond as a covalent bond whose shared pair is donated by one atom.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the one-atom source of the shared pair.

rubric.why: Identifies the lone pair used to make the coordinate bond.
rubric.description: States that the donor atom supplies a lone pair of electrons.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for mentioning the donor’s lone pair.

rubric.why: Identifies the substances used in the ammonium-ion example.
rubric.description: Names or writes ammonia and a hydrogen ion as the reactants in the example.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying both reactants.

rubric.why: Checks the correct formation of the ammonium ion.
rubric.description: Writes or states that ammonia and a hydrogen ion form NH₄⁺.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct equation or equivalent statement.

rubric.why: Checks that the student identifies the donor atom and its role in forming the bond.
rubric.description: Explains that nitrogen donates its lone pair to H⁺ to form the coordinate bond.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly describing the donation and bond formation.

modelAnswer: A coordinate covalent bond is a covalent bond in which both electrons of the shared pair are donated by the same atom.
The donor atom supplies a lone pair of electrons; the receiving atom accepts that pair.
For example, ammonia has a lone pair on its nitrogen atom, and a hydrogen ion can accept this pair.
NH₃ + H⁺ → NH₄⁺
Nitrogen donates its lone pair to H⁺ to form a coordinate covalent bond in the ammonium ion.

items.followUp: Write balanced equations for the reactions of sodium with water, oxygen, hydrogen and chlorine.

rubric.why: Tests the balanced equation for sodium reacting with water.
rubric.description: Writes the balanced equation forming sodium hydroxide and hydrogen from sodium and water.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct balanced equation.

rubric.why: Tests the balanced equation for sodium reacting with oxygen.
rubric.description: Writes the balanced equation forming sodium oxide from sodium and oxygen.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct balanced equation.

rubric.why: Tests the balanced equation for sodium reacting with hydrogen.
rubric.description: Writes the balanced equation forming sodium hydride from sodium and hydrogen.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct balanced equation.

rubric.why: Tests the balanced equation for sodium reacting with chlorine.
rubric.description: Writes the balanced equation forming sodium chloride from sodium and chlorine.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct balanced equation.

modelAnswer: With water: 2Na + 2H₂O → 2NaOH + H₂
With oxygen: 4Na + O₂ → 2Na₂O
With hydrogen: 2Na + H₂ → 2NaH
With chlorine: 2Na + Cl₂ → 2NaCl

items.followUp: Write the empirical formulae of ethene and glucose.

rubric.why: Tests the empirical formula of silica.
rubric.description: Gives SiO₂ as the empirical formula of silica.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct formula.

rubric.why: Tests the simplest whole-number ratio of carbon to hydrogen in benzene.
rubric.description: Gives CH as the empirical formula of benzene.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct formula.

modelAnswer: The empirical formula of silica is SiO₂.
The empirical formula of benzene is CH.
